source_line: Reliable speed forecasts support traffic management, route guidance, and other intelligent transportation system functions. Long-distance highways present a particular sensing problem because continuous roadside detection is expensive to deploy and maintain over large spatial extents. Floating car data (FCD) offer a practical alternative by providing speed and travel-time information without a dense network of fixed detectors. Recent work has used FCD for speed estimation, congestion analysis, traffic-state monitoring, and forecasting \cite{Zhang2025FCD}. Commercial FCD have also been combined with lower-cost sensing sources where conventional monitoring is limited \cite{Ipekyuz2025FCD}. The remaining question for forecasting is not simply whether FCD are available, but whether the observations returned by a commercial service can be converted into a consistent and auditable time series.

source_line: Commercial FCD differ from conventional detector data in several ways that matter for evaluation. Services such as TomTom provide provider-processed speed and travel-time estimates through an application programming interface (API) rather than raw vehicle trajectories, leaving upstream sampling, map matching, aggregation, and filtering outside the user's control. More importantly, a planned node--time observation may be absent from the API response altogether rather than appearing as an explicit null. The Pan Borneo Highway dataset used here illustrates this problem: 51 fixed virtual nodes cover an approximately 130-km corridor, but observations are spatially discrete and their temporal coverage, confidence, and gap lengths vary by node and time. If returned rows are treated as a complete series, unreturned observations disappear from the denominator and the distinction among missing, quality-ineligible, and imputed values becomes unclear. That ambiguity can change which forecast origins are available to each model.

source_line: Commercial FCD differ from conventional detector data in several ways that matter for evaluation. Services such as TomTom provide provider-processed speed and travel-time estimates through an application programming interface (API) rather than raw vehicle trajectories, leaving upstream sampling, map matching, aggregation, and filtering outside the user's control. More importantly, a planned node--time observation may be absent from the API response altogether rather than appearing as an explicit null. The Pan Borneo Highway dataset used here illustrates this problem: 51 fixed virtual nodes cover an approximately 130-km corridor, but observations are spatially discrete and their temporal coverage, confidence, and gap lengths vary by node and time. If returned rows are treated as a complete series, unreturned observations disappear from the denominator and the distinction among missing, quality-ineligible, and imputed values becomes unclear. That ambiguity can change which forecast origins are available to each model.

source_line: Prior research addresses the main components of this problem, but usually in separate workflows. Commercial and vehicle-level FCD have been used for traffic-state estimation and prediction \cite{Ipekyuz2025FCD,Yu2024AutoformerFCD}. Multi-horizon studies have compared naive, statistical, machine-learning, and deep-learning models and have shown that relative performance can change with forecast horizon \cite{Hadry2025TrafficForecasting,Zeb2024FeatureProjection}. A separate body of work treats incomplete traffic observations through completion, imputation, or joint prediction--imputation methods \cite{Chen2024TrafficCompletion,Bikram2024Imputation,Qu2024TrafficPredictionImputation,Zhang2024MissingData}. These strands provide the necessary methods, but they do not by themselves ensure that sparse API-derived FCD are evaluated on a fixed observation space, with the same forecast cases and the same temporal information boundaries across models.

source_line: Applying these methods to sparse commercial FCD exposes three evaluation problems. Planned node--time combinations must first be reconstructed before completeness and eligibility can be measured. Model comparisons can otherwise be confounded if different predictors retain different origins or use different missing-value treatments. Temporal order also has to be enforced inside preprocessing: a chronological train--test split does not prevent leakage if normalization, imputation, or feature statistics use information unavailable at the forecast origin \cite{Hewamalage2023ForecastEvaluation}. Finally, one test interval and one mean error cannot show whether a small model advantage persists across time, locations, forecast horizons, or history-reliability conditions. When differences between simple and complex models are small, stability under common causal samples is more informative than the mean ranking alone.

source_line: The analysis addresses three questions: (i) can sparse API-derived FCD support 1-, 3-, and 6-h future-window mean-speed forecasting after explicit observation and target eligibility checks; (ii) how do Historical Average (HA), Seasonal Historical Average (SeasonalHA), Persistence, Ridge, XGBoost, and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) compare when they use identical forecast origins and target definitions; and (iii) how stable are those comparisons across rolling-origin folds, random seeds, and history-reliability conditions? We address these questions with the Grid-Reconstructed, Auditable, Temporally Causal, and Eligibility-Gated Multi-Horizon FCD Forecasting framework (GATE-FCD). GATE-FCD reconstructs the planned node--time grid, distinguishes missing and quality-ineligible observations, creates a causal 24-h history, and freezes a common sample manifest before model fitting. Six models are then evaluated across six retrospective rolling-origin folds and three horizons. This design isolates differences in forecasting behavior from differences in sample composition and makes it possible to examine where a small accuracy gain is stable and where it reverses.
